title: Sysadmin Skills Test
description: 250 multiple-choice questions covering Linux/Unix system administration, networking, DevOps, and security fundamentals, based on the test-your-sysadmin-skills question bank.

questions.q: Unix, Linux, BSD, and GNU are often mentioned together. Which of these is NOT actually an operating system itself, but rather a project/philosophy that produced tools later combined with a kernel?
questions.correct: GNU
questions.explain: GNU is a set of free-software tools and principles, not an OS by itself; it became an OS only when combined with a kernel (e.g. Linux, forming GNU/Linux).

questions.q: Which command displays the full manual page for another command?
questions.correct: man
questions.explain: `man` shows the full manual page; `apropos`/`whatis` only search/show one-line descriptions, and `info` uses a different documentation system.

questions.q: Which single command gives you server uptime, load average, and a list of logged-in users all in one view?
questions.correct: w
questions.explain: `w` combines uptime, load average, and logged-in user info; `who` lacks load/uptime, `uptime` lacks user info, and `last` only shows login history.

questions.q: In the output of `ls -al`, what does the second field (after the permissions string) represent?
questions.correct: the number of hard links
questions.explain: The second field in `ls -al` output is the hard link count, not the inode number (which requires `-i`) or a directory count.

questions.q: Which command gives a simple summary of currently logged-in users (username, terminal, login time) without CPU or idle-time detail?
questions.correct: who
questions.explain: `who` gives the simple summary; `w` adds CPU/idle info, `last` shows historical logins, and `users` only lists usernames with no detail.

questions.q: Which special character, appended to the end of a command, sends it to run in the background?
questions.explain: A trailing `&` backgrounds a job; `&&` chains commands conditionally, `|` pipes output, and `;` just separates sequential commands.

questions.q: Why is routinely running commands as the root user considered bad practice?
questions.correct: It removes the safety pause sudo provides and increases the damage a single mistake can cause
distractors: It makes every command run noticeably slower due to extra permission checks
It is only risky on multi-user systems, not single-user workstations
Actions taken as root are always fully logged automatically, so there's no real risk
questions.explain: Running as root removes the deliberate pause/audit step sudo provides and means any mistake has full-system consequences; the other options misstate how root and logging actually work.

questions.q: Which pair of commands is the standard way to check physical and virtual memory statistics on Linux?
questions.correct: free and vmstat
questions.explain: `free` and `vmstat` report physical/virtual memory stats directly; `top`/`htop` are process monitors, and `iostat`/`mpstat` focus on disk/CPU stats.

questions.q: Linux load average is typically reported as an average over which three time windows?
questions.correct: 1, 5, and 15 minutes
questions.explain: Standard load average output uses 1-, 5-, and 15-minute windows; the other groupings are close but not the real intervals.

questions.q: Where are Linux user password hashes actually stored?
questions.correct: /etc/shadow
questions.explain: Password hashes live in /etc/shadow (readable only by root); /etc/passwd historically held account info but not the hash on modern systems.

questions.q: Which command recursively sets permissions on only directories (not files) under /opt/data?
questions.correct: find /opt/data -type d -exec chmod 755 {} \;
questions.explain: The `-type d` test limits the find to directories; plain `chmod -R` would hit files too, `-type f` targets files instead, and `--dirs-only` isn't a real chmod flag.

questions.q: If every command suddenly fails with "command not found", which environment variable has most likely been overwritten or corrupted?
questions.correct: PATH
questions.explain: PATH tells the shell where to look for executables; LD_LIBRARY_PATH affects shared libraries, PS1 is just the prompt, and HOME is the user's home directory.

questions.q: Which signal does pressing CTRL+C send to the foreground process?
questions.correct: SIGINT
questions.explain: CTRL+C sends SIGINT; CTRL+\ sends SIGQUIT, SIGTERM/SIGKILL are sent by the `kill` command, not a terminal keystroke.

questions.q: Which grep option lets you match multiple alternative patterns in one command, e.g. `grep -E "string1|string2" file`?
questions.correct: -E
questions.explain: `-E` enables extended regex so `|` works as alternation; `-e` just supplies an additional pattern, `-F` treats patterns as fixed strings, and `-P` enables Perl regex.

questions.q: Which command lets you view a text file with both backward scrolling and single-line movement in the terminal?
questions.correct: less
questions.explain: `less` supports backward and line-by-line navigation; `more` is more limited (forward paging mostly), `cat` dumps the whole file, and `tail` only shows the end.

questions.q: Which POSIX signal is traditionally sent to a process when its controlling terminal closes, and which many daemons use as a cue to reload configuration?
questions.correct: SIGHUP
questions.explain: SIGHUP ("hangup") was originally for serial line drops and is now commonly repurposed by daemons for config reload; the others are interrupt/terminate/quit signals with different triggers.

questions.q: When you run `kill <pid>` with no signal specified, which signal is sent by default?
questions.correct: SIGTERM (15)
questions.explain: The default is SIGTERM, a polite request to terminate that a process can catch/handle; SIGKILL cannot be caught and must be requested explicitly with `-9`.

questions.q: Compared to plain `rm`, what does adding `-f` (force) to `rm -r` do?
questions.correct: It ignores nonexistent files and suppresses confirmation prompts
distractors: It forces deletion of read-only directories only, leaving files untouched
It forces a filesystem sync before the delete completes
It follows symbolic links and deletes their targets
questions.explain: `-f` suppresses prompts and errors about missing files; it doesn't change how symlinks or read-only directories specifically are handled.

questions.q: Which command lists the contents of `archive.tgz` without extracting anything?
questions.correct: tar tf archive.tgz
questions.explain: The `t` flag lists contents; `x` extracts, `c` creates a new archive, and `d` (diff) compares archive contents to the filesystem.

questions.q: Which operator runs the next command only if the previous command succeeded (exit code 0)?
questions.explain: `&&` is conditional on success; `;` runs commands regardless of outcome, `||` runs the next command only if the previous one failed, and `|` pipes output between commands.

questions.q: Which command grants execute permission to all users on a file without altering its other existing permission bits?
questions.correct: chmod a+x file
questions.explain: `a+x` adds only the execute bit for all classes; `777` overwrites all permissions, `u+x` only affects the owner, and `+rwx` (no class) still expands to all classes and all three bits, not just execute.

questions.q: Which rsync flags make dir2 an exact mirror of dir1, removing files from dir2 that no longer exist in dir1?
questions.correct: -av --delete
questions.explain: `--delete` removes extraneous destination files; `--update` skips overwriting newer destination files instead, `--backup` preserves old versions rather than deleting, and `--exclude` needs a pattern and doesn't mirror deletions on its own.

questions.q: What is generally considered the best practice for tracking and reverting changes to system configuration files over time?
questions.correct: Use version control such as git (e.g. etckeeper for /etc)
distractors: Keep a single .bak copy of the file in the same directory
Rely on your text editor's undo history
Take a full system snapshot before every single edit
questions.explain: Version control gives a full, searchable history of changes; a single backup copy or editor undo history is fragile and doesn't scale, and full snapshots are far heavier than needed for config tracking.

questions.q: Which find command lists all regular files larger than 20MB under /?
questions.correct: find / -type f -size +20M
questions.explain: `-size +20M` means larger than 20MB; `-size -20M` means smaller, `-type d` would only match directories, and `20MB` (with a lowercase b) isn't valid find syntax.

questions.q: What specifically does the trailing `-` do in `sudo su -` that plain `sudo su` doesn't?
questions.correct: It starts a login shell, resetting the environment to match the target user
distractors: It switches to root without requiring any password
It restarts the shell process without preserving login status
It only changes the prompt string, not the environment
questions.explain: `su -` invokes a login shell, resetting environment variables (PATH, HOME, etc.) to the target user's defaults; plain `su` keeps most of the calling user's environment.

questions.q: Which find command shows files modified within the last 60 minutes?
questions.correct: find / -mmin -60 -type f
questions.explain: `-mmin -60` means modified less than 60 minutes ago; `-mmin +60` means more than 60 minutes ago, `-mtime -60` uses days (not minutes) as the unit, and `-amin` checks access time, not modification time.

questions.q: What is the primary operational reason for retaining old log files?
questions.correct: They provide evidence for investigating security incidents and troubleshooting past problems
distractors: They reduce current disk I/O load
They automatically improve system performance over time
They are required to satisfy filesystem journaling
questions.explain: Logs are a historical record used for investigation and troubleshooting; they have no effect on current I/O, performance, or journaling.

questions.q: What defines an incremental backup?
questions.correct: It backs up only the data that changed since the last backup of any type (full or incremental)
distractors: It backs up only the data changed since the last full backup
It performs a full backup every time but with extra compression
It backs up only system files, never user data
questions.explain: Incremental backups chain off the most recent backup, whatever type it was; backing up only what changed since the last *full* backup is the definition of a differential backup, not incremental.

questions.q: Which RAID level uses pure mirroring (identical data written to two drives) with no striping or parity?
questions.correct: RAID1
questions.explain: RAID1 mirrors data across drives; RAID0 stripes data with no redundancy, RAID5 uses striping with parity, and RAID10 combines mirroring and striping.

questions.q: Which `useradd` option sets a new user's initial (primary) group?
questions.correct: -g
questions.explain: `-g` sets the primary group; `-G` sets supplementary/secondary groups, `-u` sets the UID, and `-d` sets the home directory.

questions.q: Which of the following is a commonly cited reason for rack-mounting servers?
questions.correct: Better cooling and airflow management
questions.explain: Rack mounting is about physical organization, cooling, power, and hardware protection; it has no inherent effect on load balancing, backup needs, or encryption.

questions.q: Which of these correctly describes the OSI model's core benefit for networking?
questions.correct: It divides protocols into layers, each providing abstraction and encapsulation, decoupled from other layers
distractors: It guarantees that every network device speaks the same physical protocol
It replaces the need for IP addressing with named endpoints
It ensures that all layers must be implemented for any network to function
questions.explain: The OSI model's value is layering/abstraction/encapsulation and decoupling of functions - it doesn't dictate physical protocols, replace IP addressing, or require every layer be implemented.

questions.q: What layer of the network stack do VLANs primarily operate at, versus subnets?
questions.correct: VLANs work at Layer 2, subnets are a Layer 3 concept
distractors: VLANs work at Layer 3, subnets are a Layer 2 concept
Both VLANs and subnets operate strictly at Layer 3
Both VLANs and subnets operate strictly at Layer 2
questions.explain: VLANs alter Layer 2 broadcast domains, while subnets are defined by Layer 3 IP addressing and netmasks.

questions.q: Which port does SSH use by default?
questions.explain: SSH's default port is 22; 21 is FTP control, 23 is Telnet, and 25 is SMTP.

questions.q: Which protocol, by default, downloads mail to the client and removes it from the server (unless configured otherwise)?
questions.correct: POP (Post Office Protocol)
questions.explain: POP traditionally pulls mail down and removes it from the server; IMAP instead keeps mail synced on the server, and SMTP is for sending, not retrieving, mail.

questions.q: Which command(s) can show the current default route and routing table on Linux?
questions.correct: netstat -nr, route -n, or ip route show
questions.explain: netstat -nr, route -n, and ip route show all display routing tables; ss shows socket info, traceroute shows the path to a host, and arp shows the MAC/IP cache, not routes.

questions.q: Why does using 127.0.0.1 sometimes behave differently from using 'localhost' in an application?
questions.correct: 'localhost' requires a name lookup/resolution step, while 127.0.0.1 can be used directly as an IP without resolving anything
distractors: 127.0.0.1 only works over IPv6, while localhost only works over IPv4
'localhost' always bypasses the network stack entirely, unlike 127.0.0.1
127.0.0.1 requires DNS to be configured correctly, unlike localhost
questions.explain: 127.0.0.1 is already an IP address and can skip resolution; 'localhost' still needs to be resolved (typically via /etc/hosts or DNS), and there's no guarantee of how that resolution is configured.

questions.q: What protocol does the `ping` command actually use, given that it has no associated TCP/UDP port?
questions.correct: ICMP (echo request/echo reply)
questions.explain: ping uses ICMP echo request/reply packets, identified by the protocol field in the IP header, not a TCP/UDP port; ARP is a separate protocol for MAC address resolution.

questions.q: When troubleshooting 'Server A can't talk to Server B', which layer should you check first if you suspect the application itself isn't listening or is misconfigured?
questions.correct: Application layer
questions.explain: Confirming the service is up, correctly bound, and free of application/log errors is an application-layer check, before moving down the stack to transport (ports/telnet) and network (routing/ping) layers.

questions.q: Which command-line tool is used specifically to test TCP port connectivity to a remote host, alongside `nc -vz`?
questions.correct: telnet
questions.explain: telnet (or `nc -vz`) can test whether a specific TCP port is reachable; ping only tests ICMP reachability, traceroute maps the path, and dig performs DNS lookups.

questions.q: Why is telnet discouraged for remotely administering systems?
questions.correct: It transmits data, including login credentials, in plain text over the network
distractors: It only supports IPv4 and cannot be used on modern networks
It cannot be used to test port connectivity
It requires a paid license on most operating systems
questions.explain: Telnet's core weakness is sending everything, including passwords, unencrypted; it has nothing to do with IPv4/IPv6 support or licensing, and it's actually still useful for testing port connectivity.

questions.q: Which tool is better known for its ability to download files and directories recursively?
questions.correct: wget
questions.explain: wget's strong point is recursive downloading; curl supports far more protocols but isn't focused on recursive downloads, while scp/rsync are file-transfer tools, not general download utilities.

questions.q: Why is SSH key authentication generally considered more secure than password authentication?
questions.correct: It uses asymmetric cryptography (public/private key pairs) instead of a guessable or brute-forceable secret
distractors: It automatically encrypts all files on the remote server
It disables root login on the server by default
It requires two-factor authentication built into the protocol
questions.explain: SSH keys rely on asymmetric cryptography rather than a password that could be guessed or brute-forced; key auth doesn't itself encrypt files, disable root login, or mandate 2FA.

questions.q: What does packet filtering, as a firewall technique, base its allow/deny decisions on?
questions.correct: Source/destination IP addresses, protocols, and ports
distractors: The content and payload of each packet
The reputation score of the sending domain
questions.explain: Packet filtering inspects IP/protocol/port headers, not payload content, domain reputation, or file types (that's more the domain of deep packet inspection or application-layer firewalls).

questions.q: What is a key advantage of placing a reverse proxy in front of backend servers?
questions.correct: It hides the topology and characteristics of the backend servers from clients
distractors: It eliminates the need for TLS/SSL certificates entirely
It guarantees zero downtime during backend maintenance automatically
It replaces the need for a firewall
questions.explain: Reverse proxies obscure backend details and can enable transparent maintenance, but they don't remove the need for TLS, guarantee zero-downtime deploys by themselves, or replace a firewall.

questions.q: What best describes the relationship between a 'router' and the 'default gateway' on a LAN?
questions.correct: The default gateway is the specific router responsible for forwarding a host's traffic destined for other networks
distractors: A default gateway is any device on the LAN, router or not, that has an IP address
A router only operates within a single subnet and never forwards traffic elsewhere
The default gateway and router always refer to two physically separate devices
questions.explain: 'Router' describes the layer-3 forwarding function/device in general, while 'default gateway' specifically names the router handling a given host's off-subnet traffic; they're often the same device.

questions.q: Which DNS record type maps a domain name to an IPv4 address?
questions.correct: A record
questions.explain: An A record maps a name to an IPv4 address; AAAA does the same for IPv6, CNAME is an alias to another name, and PTR does reverse (IP-to-name) lookups.

questions.q: Which DNS record type is used for reverse lookups (mapping an IP address back to a hostname)?
questions.correct: PTR record
questions.explain: PTR records handle reverse DNS; A records go name-to-IP (the opposite direction), MX records route mail, and SOA holds authority/zone metadata.

questions.q: Why can't MAC addresses simply replace IP addresses for internet-wide routing?
questions.correct: MAC addresses are a Layer 2 mechanism meant for communication within a local physical network, while routing across networks is a Layer 3 function
distractors: MAC addresses are not unique enough to identify individual devices
MAC addresses can only be assigned by an ISP, unlike IP addresses
MAC addresses cannot be read by networking hardware, only by the OS
questions.explain: Routing decisions are inherently a Layer 3 (IP) job; MAC addresses are Layer 2 and only meaningful for a device's immediate physical segment.

questions.q: What is the smallest IPv4 subnet (CIDR prefix) that can accommodate up to 30 host devices?
questions.explain: A /27 provides 32 addresses (30 usable hosts after network/broadcast); /28 only gives 16 addresses (14 usable), too few, while /24 and /26 are larger than necessary.

questions.q: In HTTP status codes, which range indicates that the error is on the client's side?
questions.correct: 4xx
questions.explain: 4xx codes point to client-side errors (e.g. 404 Not Found); 5xx are server-side errors, 3xx are redirections, and 2xx indicate success.

questions.q: Which best captures what version control systems fundamentally provide?
questions.correct: The ability to record and recall changes to files over time, including reverting to previous states
distractors: Automatic deployment of code to production servers
Automatic testing of code before every commit
Real-time chat between team members about code changes
questions.explain: Version control's core job is tracking and recalling historical file states; deployment, automated testing, and team chat are separate tooling concerns (CI/CD, test frameworks, chat apps).

questions.q: Which git command creates a brand-new local repository?
questions.correct: git init
questions.explain: `git init` creates a new repo from scratch; `git clone` copies an existing remote repo, `git status` shows working tree state, and `git commit` records staged changes.

questions.q: Which git command sends your committed local changes to the master branch of a remote repository?
questions.correct: git push origin master
questions.explain: `git push` uploads commits to the remote; `git commit` only records changes locally, `git status` just reports state, and `git init` creates a new repo.

questions.q: In a simple Continuous Integration pipeline, what typically happens right after the repository is cloned?
questions.correct: The code is deployed to a QA/testing stage before production
distractors: The code is immediately deployed straight to production
The pipeline waits indefinitely for manual code review before any deployment step
questions.explain: A basic CI pipeline moves through QA/testing stages before reaching production, rather than deploying straight to prod or skipping testing.

questions.q: Which docker command lists only the currently running containers (not stopped ones)?
questions.correct: docker ps
questions.explain: Plain `docker ps` shows running containers only; `-a` adds stopped ones, `docker images` lists images (not containers), and `docker logs` shows a specific container's log output.

questions.q: Which docker command opens an interactive bash shell inside a running container?
questions.correct: docker exec -it <container> bash
questions.explain: `docker exec -it ... bash` attaches an interactive shell; `docker logs` only shows output, `docker ps -a` lists containers, and `docker network ls` lists networks.

questions.q: What is a security misconfiguration?
questions.correct: A vulnerability where a device, application, or network is set up in a way an attacker can exploit, such as leaving default credentials unchanged
distractors: A flaw in the underlying source code of an application
A vulnerability that only affects cloud-hosted systems
A type of malware that reconfigures firewall rules automatically
questions.explain: Security misconfiguration is about insecure setup/configuration choices (like default passwords), not a code-level flaw, a cloud-only issue, or malware.

questions.q: In the classic BIOS boot process, what runs immediately before the bootloader is loaded?
questions.correct: BIOS performs integrity checks (POST) and locates the boot device
distractors: The kernel initializes all hardware drivers
The init/systemd process starts user-space services
questions.explain: BIOS/POST integrity checks happen first and hand off to the bootloader; kernel driver init, init/systemd, and filesystem mounting all happen later in the boot sequence.

questions.q: On a single-core machine, why do many sysadmins treat a load average of 1.00 as a 'fix this now' threshold?
questions.correct: A load of 1.00 means the single CPU has no spare headroom left
distractors: A load of 1.00 always means the CPU is at 10% utilization
A load of 1.00 indicates the system has crashed
A load of 1.00 only matters on multi-core systems, not single-core
questions.explain: On a single core, a load average of 1.00 means demand exactly matches capacity, leaving no headroom; it doesn't indicate a crash or low utilization, and it applies specifically because there's only one core to divide the load across.

questions.q: If your effective user ID is root but your real user ID is still your own username, what does that indicate?
questions.correct: A setuid mechanism is temporarily elevating your privileges for permission checks while your real identity is preserved
distractors: You have permanently switched to the root account
The system has a corrupted /etc/passwd file
Your session has two separate users logged in simultaneously
questions.explain: The real UID tracks who you actually are, while the effective UID (elevated via setuid) is what's checked for permissions - this is a normal, intentional mechanism, not a corruption or dual-login state.

questions.q: A cron job is generating massive log files. What is the standard tool/approach for managing this going forward?
questions.correct: logrotate, configured via a new file under /etc/logrotate.d/
distractors: Editing /etc/logrotate.conf directly with your custom job
Manually deleting the log file every day with a new cron job
Disabling logging for that cron job entirely
questions.explain: Best practice is adding your own file under /etc/logrotate.d/ rather than editing the main logrotate.conf, which would complicate future upgrades; manual deletion or disabling logging loses useful data.

questions.q: In `top`, which interactive key sorts the process list by current (instantaneous) CPU usage?
questions.correct: P
questions.explain: P sorts by current CPU usage; M sorts by resident memory usage, T sorts by cumulative/total CPU usage, and ? shows a help/usage summary.

questions.q: What is the best-practice approach for upgrading the ntpd service consistently across 200 servers?
questions.correct: Use a configuration management / Infrastructure as Code tool (e.g. Ansible, Chef, Puppet, SaltStack)
distractors: SSH into each server manually and run the upgrade one at a time
Write a single shell script and email it to each server owner to run
Rely on each server's automatic OS updates to eventually catch it
questions.explain: Configuration management tools give repeatable, auditable, automated upgrades across many servers; manual SSH sessions or ad hoc scripts don't scale reliably, and automatic OS updates typically skip major/minor version bumps by design.

questions.q: Where can kernel-generated boot messages (via printk) always be found, viewable with the `dmesg` command?
questions.correct: The kmsg buffer
questions.explain: Kernel messages are always stored in the kmsg ring buffer, viewable via dmesg, and are often copied to syslog; they aren't tied exclusively to one particular log file or to bash history.

questions.q: What condition typically triggers the Linux kernel to start moving inactive memory pages into swap space?
questions.correct: Available RAM has been fully utilized
distractors: The system has been running for more than 24 hours
questions.explain: Swapping is triggered by memory pressure (RAM being fully used), not by uptime, CPU usage, or disk I/O wait alone.

questions.q: What does `umask` control?
questions.correct: The default permission bits masked out (removed) when new files/directories are created
distractors: The maximum file size a user is allowed to create
The default owner assigned to new files
The encryption algorithm used for new files
questions.explain: umask subtracts permission bits from the system default at creation time; it has no bearing on max file size, default ownership, or encryption.

questions.q: With a umask of 022, what permissions result on a newly created regular file (starting from a 666 base)?
questions.explain: 022 removes write for group and other from the 666 base, giving 644; 755 would apply to directories (base 777), 600 corresponds to a stricter umask like 077, and 664 corresponds to umask 002.

questions.q: What underlying filesystem structure do both hard links and the original filename actually point to?
questions.correct: An inode
questions.explain: Both a file's name and any hard links to it point to the same inode, which is only freed once all links to it are removed; superblocks and extended attribute blocks serve different filesystem purposes.

questions.q: What happens when a symbolic link's target file is deleted, compared to what happens to a hard link in the same situation?
questions.correct: The symbolic link becomes a dangling/broken link, whereas a hard link still points to valid data via the shared inode as long as one link remains
distractors: Both the symbolic link and hard link become broken and unusable
The symbolic link is automatically deleted along with the target
Deleting the target file is prevented entirely if any symlink references it
questions.explain: A symlink references the target by name/path, so it breaks if the target's name goes away; a hard link references the inode directly and survives as long as at least one link (name) to that inode still exists.

questions.q: Are the SUID/SGID bits and the sticky bit the same permission mechanism?
questions.correct: No - they are two completely different mechanisms, both occupying special positions in a file's permission bits
distractors: Yes, SUID/SGID and the sticky bit are just two names for the same bit
Yes, but SUID only applies to directories while the sticky bit only applies to files
No, but only one of them can be set on a given file at any time
questions.explain: SUID/SGID affect how a program's effective user/group ID is set on execution, while the sticky bit (traditionally on directories like /tmp) restricts file deletion to the owner; they are distinct mechanisms and can coexist.

questions.q: What is the main practical reason to prefix a command with `LC_ALL=C`?
questions.correct: To force plain/English locale behavior and often speed up text-processing commands like grep
distractors: To permanently change the system's default locale for all users
To disable all environment variables for the command
To force the command to run with root privileges
questions.explain: LC_ALL=C overrides locale settings for that command only (not permanently) and can speed up text processing; it doesn't touch privileges or clear all environment variables.

questions.q: In BSD, what is the purpose of booting into single-user mode after forgetting the root password?
questions.correct: It provides a root shell prompt directly, letting you remount the filesystem read-write and reset the password
distractors: It boots a completely separate recovery operating system from a USB drive
It automatically emails the root password to a configured recovery address
It permanently disables password authentication for root
questions.explain: Single-user mode drops you to a root prompt so you can remount root read-write and run passwd; it doesn't involve a separate OS, email recovery, or permanently disabling authentication.

questions.q: Which command lets you write content directly into a file without opening a text editor, e.g. `cat > filename << __EOF__`?
questions.correct: cat
questions.explain: A heredoc combined with `cat >` (or `>>`) writes content to a file without an editor; vim/less are editors/pagers, and while `tee` can also write files, the example shown specifically uses `cat`.

questions.q: After editing /etc/sysctl.conf to change kernel parameters, which command applies the changes without rebooting?
questions.correct: sysctl -p
questions.explain: `sysctl -p` reloads settings from sysctl.conf immediately; the other commands either don't exist as shown or would force an unnecessary reboot (init 6).

questions.q: What best describes the /proc filesystem?
questions.correct: A virtual filesystem exposing real-time kernel, hardware, and process information, with most files reporting zero byte size
distractors: A physical partition storing process executables
A backup location for deleted process data
A configuration directory read only once at boot
questions.explain: /proc is virtual and dynamically generated (not a physical partition or static config), giving a live view of kernel/process state, which is why files like /proc/meminfo show 0 bytes in `ls`.

questions.q: In ext3/ext4 journaling modes, which mode journals both metadata AND file content?
questions.correct: Journal mode
questions.explain: Journal mode logs both data and metadata; Ordered mode (the default) only journals metadata but writes data first, and Writeback mode only journals metadata with no strict ordering guarantee.

questions.q: What information does a Linux inode store about a file?
questions.correct: All file metadata (permissions, owner, timestamps, size, pointers to data blocks) except the filename and the actual data itself
distractors: The file's name and its full content
questions.explain: The inode holds nearly all metadata but notably NOT the filename (that's stored in the directory entry) or the data itself (stored in data blocks).

questions.q: If `ls -l` shows question marks instead of real file attributes, what is the most likely underlying cause?
questions.correct: The user can read the directory listing but cannot stat() the individual files, often due to missing execute permission on the directory
distractors: The filesystem itself is corrupted beyond repair
The files have been encrypted and require a passphrase
ls is simply an outdated version that needs upgrading
questions.explain: Question marks typically appear when directory read access exists but execute (needed for stat()) doesn't, producing permission-denied-style errors on a per-file basis rather than full corruption, encryption, or a tooling bug.

questions.q: Which of these is a genuine benefit of using LVM (Logical Volume Management)?
questions.correct: It lets you resize, move, and snapshot logical volumes across physical volumes without unmounting them
distractors: It automatically encrypts all data stored on the volume
It eliminates the need for regular backups
It doubles disk write speed compared to raw partitions
questions.explain: LVM's real strengths are flexible resizing, moving, mirroring, and snapshotting; it does not provide encryption, remove the need for backups, or inherently speed up writes.

questions.q: Which command is used to grow the size of an existing LVM logical volume?
questions.correct: lvextend
questions.explain: `lvextend` grows the logical volume itself; `lvcreate` makes a new volume, `resize2fs` grows the ext filesystem on top of an already-extended volume, and `vgextend` adds a physical volume to a volume group, not to a logical volume directly.

questions.q: What is a 'zombie' (defunct) process?
questions.correct: A process that has finished executing but still has an entry in the process table because its parent hasn't reaped it
distractors: A process that is stuck in an infinite loop consuming CPU
A process that has been forcibly killed with SIGKILL but won't release memory
A process running with corrupted binary code
questions.explain: A zombie has already terminated - it's just an unreaped table entry waiting for its parent (or init) to collect its exit status; it isn't consuming CPU or memory, and it isn't a code corruption issue.

questions.q: What is a key benefit of running `mysql_secure_installation` after installing MySQL?
questions.correct: It lets you set the root password and remove anonymous accounts and the default test database
distractors: It automatically encrypts all existing databases
It upgrades MySQL to the latest major version
questions.explain: mysql_secure_installation hardens the default install (root password, anonymous accounts, test DB) - it doesn't encrypt data, upgrade versions, or set up backups.

questions.q: According to standard best practice for stopping a misbehaving process, which signal should you try FIRST, before escalating?
questions.correct: SIGTERM (kill -15)
questions.explain: SIGTERM is the polite, first-attempt signal that allows clean shutdown; SIGKILL should be a last resort since it can't be caught and may leave things in a bad state, and SIGHUP/SIGSTOP serve different purposes (reload/pause).

questions.q: What does `strace` fundamentally do when attached to a running process?
questions.correct: It captures and logs the system calls made by the process, and the signals it receives
distractors: It recompiles the process's binary with debug symbols
It measures only the process's network bandwidth usage
It automatically restarts the process if it crashes
questions.explain: strace monitors syscalls and signals for debugging purposes; it doesn't recompile binaries, focus solely on network bandwidth, or provide automatic restart/supervision.

questions.q: Which hashing algorithms are considered outdated and should NOT be used for password security in /etc/shadow anymore?
questions.correct: MD5 and SHA-1
questions.explain: MD5 and SHA-1 are considered cryptographically weak for this purpose; SHA-256/512/3 remain in current use, and bcrypt/Argon2 are modern password-hashing algorithms (not the ones being deprecated here).

questions.q: What is the purpose of `ulimit` on Unix-like systems?
questions.correct: To limit and control per-process/per-user usage of system resources like open files and processes
distractors: To limit the maximum disk quota per user
To set the maximum CPU clock speed available to a process
To restrict which commands a user is allowed to run
questions.explain: ulimit controls resource usage limits (file descriptors, processes, memory, etc.) per process/user; it doesn't manage disk quotas, CPU clock speed, or command permissions (that's more the domain of sudoers or SELinux).

questions.q: What is the difference between a soft limit and a hard limit for user resource usage?
questions.correct: A hard limit is the absolute maximum set by root; a user can raise their own soft limit up to, but not beyond, that hard limit
distractors: A soft limit is set by root and cannot be changed by the user at all
A hard limit only applies to disk space, while soft limits apply to everything else
Soft and hard limits are identical, just stored in different config files
questions.explain: Hard limits are the ceiling set by root in limits.conf; soft limits are user-adjustable but capped at the hard limit - they aren't restricted to disk space or interchangeable concepts.

questions.q: You get 'Server refused our key' when trying RSA key-based SSH login. Where should you look first on the server side to diagnose it?
questions.correct: SSH auth logs (e.g. /var/log/auth.log, /var/log/secure) after raising sshd's LogLevel to VERBOSE
questions.explain: Server-side auth logs (with verbose sshd logging) show exactly why a key was rejected; known_hosts is client-side host verification, resolv.conf is DNS config, and shell history isn't related to SSH auth failures.

questions.q: Which command generates a file of 100 lines of random alphanumeric values using /dev/urandom?
questions.correct: cat /dev/urandom | tr -dc 'a-zA-Z0-9' | fold -w 32 | head -n 100 > file
questions.explain: /dev/urandom supplies actual random bytes filtered to alphanumerics; /dev/null produces no data, /dev/zero produces all zero bytes, and $RANDOM alone isn't the shown technique for generating file content lines.

questions.q: Using visudo, how do you allow user1 to run a specific script as user2 without being prompted for a password?
questions.correct: user1 ALL=(user2) NOPASSWD: /opt/scripts/bin/generate.sh
questions.explain: The NOPASSWD directive scoped to a specific user and absolute script path grants exactly the needed access; the other entries either grant far broader access than intended or still require a password.

questions.q: In a bash script, which variable is the recommended way to reliably check if the script is running as root, rather than checking the username?
questions.correct: $EUID
questions.explain: $EUID reflects the effective user ID (accounting for setuid), while $UID may not reflect elevated privileges the same way, and $USER/$LOGNAME are just usernames, which aren't guaranteed to be 'root' for the superuser account.

questions.q: Why might running multiple daemons as the shared 'nobody' account reduce the security benefit of using that account?
questions.correct: If one daemon is compromised, it could potentially interfere with the other daemons since they share the same limited-privilege identity
distractors: The 'nobody' account cannot be used by more than one process at a time by design
Running multiple daemons as 'nobody' automatically disables logging for all of them
The 'nobody' account requires a unique password per daemon
questions.explain: Sharing 'nobody' across daemons means a compromise of one could affect the others through that shared identity; there's no inherent one-process limitation, logging change, or password requirement tied to 'nobody'.

questions.q: Which command lets you redirect a program's stdout to a file while still displaying it live in the terminal?
questions.correct: tee
questions.explain: `tee` splits output to both a file and stdout simultaneously; `cat` just concatenates/displays, `xargs` builds commands from input, and `tail -f` follows an existing file rather than capturing live command output.

questions.q: Why is `#!/usr/bin/env bash` generally preferred over a hardcoded `#!/bin/bash` shebang?
questions.correct: It's more portable since bash may be installed in different locations across different *nix systems, and env finds it on PATH
distractors: It forces the script to run with root privileges
It makes the script run noticeably faster
It disables all environment variable inheritance for the script
questions.explain: Using env locates bash wherever it happens to live on PATH, improving portability; it has no effect on privileges, speed, or environment variable inheritance.

questions.q: How do you keep a long-running command executing after you disconnect your SSH session, without using a terminal multiplexer?
questions.correct: Prefix it with nohup, e.g. `nohup long-running-process &`
distractors: Run it with `&` alone and nothing else
Run it inside a subshell with `( )`
questions.explain: `nohup` specifically makes the process ignore the hangup (SIGHUP) signal sent when the session closes; backgrounding alone with `&` doesn't protect against SIGHUP, and `disown`/subshells serve different purposes.

questions.q: What is the main role of an Intermediate Certificate Authority in the SSL certificate trust chain?
questions.correct: It signs end-entity/server certificates on behalf of a Root CA, keeping the Root CA's private key offline and protected
distractors: It generates the private keys for all end users automatically
It replaces the need for a Root CA entirely
It only issues certificates for internal, non-public use
questions.explain: Intermediate CAs let the Root CA's key stay offline and safe while still allowing certificates to be issued and validated up the chain; they don't replace root CAs, generate user keys, or exist only for internal use.

questions.q: Which command reloads PostgreSQL configuration changes from within a SQL session, without restarting the service?
questions.correct: SELECT pg_reload_conf();
questions.explain: pg_reload_conf() applies config changes without downtime; restarting the service (or stopping it) causes an outage, and dropping the postgres database would be catastrophic and unrelated.

questions.q: After adding aliases to ~/.profile, what is the best way to reload your shell environment without logging out?
questions.correct: exec $SHELL -l
distractors: logout && login again in a script
questions.explain: `exec $SHELL -l` replaces the current shell process with a fresh login shell that re-reads profile files; rebooting is drastic overkill, and `kill -9 $$` just kills your shell rather than reloading it.

questions.q: Which of these will let you exit a shell session without saving that session's command history?
questions.correct: unset HISTFILE && exit
questions.explain: Unsetting HISTFILE before exiting prevents the shell from writing history to disk on exit; the other options either don't reliably stop the write-on-exit behavior or take drastic unrelated actions like rebooting.

questions.q: What is the 'toor' account sometimes found on BSD systems?
questions.correct: An alternative superuser account (root spelled backwards) meant to let you use a non-default shell without changing root's own shell
distractors: Evidence that the system has been compromised by an attacker
A temporary account automatically created during OS upgrades
A restricted, low-privilege backup account for root
questions.explain: toor is a legitimate, intentional alternate root-equivalent account for shell flexibility, not a sign of compromise, a temporary upgrade artifact, or a restricted account.

questions.q: Which grep flag combination recursively searches all files under the current directory for a pattern, ignoring case and suppressing errors about unreadable files?
questions.correct: grep -insr "pattern" *
questions.explain: `-i` (ignore case), `-n` (line numbers), `-s` (suppress errors), and `-r` (recursive) together match the described behavior; `-c` only counts matches, `-l` only lists filenames, and `-v` inverts the match (shows non-matching lines).

questions.q: Which command shows the dynamic/shared libraries that an executable will load at runtime?
questions.correct: ldd
questions.explain: `ldd` lists shared library dependencies; `nm` lists symbols in an object file, `strip` removes symbol/debug info, and `file` just identifies the file type.

questions.q: A monitor reports a website down, but you can successfully telnet to the port. What does that tell you?
questions.correct: The service is up and listening - the problem is likely not basic network/port connectivity, so look higher up the stack (app logic, DNS, or a specific client's path)
distractors: The service is definitely fully healthy and the monitor is simply broken
The firewall must be misconfigured to allow the connection
DNS resolution has completely failed for the domain
questions.explain: A successful telnet confirms the port is reachable and something is listening; it doesn't prove the app is fully healthy, and it rules out (rather than indicates) firewall blocking or total DNS failure at that layer.

questions.q: Which of the following is a genuine architectural difference between HTTP/2 and HTTP/1.1?
questions.correct: HTTP/2 is binary and fully multiplexed, allowing one connection to handle parallel requests
distractors: HTTP/2 is textual while HTTP/1.1 is binary
HTTP/2 removes the concept of headers entirely
HTTP/2 requires UDP instead of TCP
questions.explain: HTTP/2 switched from a textual, blocking model to binary framing with multiplexing over a single connection; it still uses headers (just compressed) and still runs over TCP (QUIC/HTTP-3 is the UDP-based successor).

questions.q: A POST request fails with 'HTTP 413 Request Entity Too Large' on an Nginx-fronted app. Which setting should you check first?
questions.correct: client_max_body_size in the Nginx config
questions.explain: client_max_body_size directly controls the maximum allowed request body size and is the classic cause of a 413; the other directives control connection handling and compression, not body size limits.

questions.q: Why does a TCP connection require a three-way handshake before data transfer begins?
questions.correct: To let both sides agree on and synchronize sequence numbers and confirm a reliable communication channel before data flows
distractors: To negotiate which application-layer protocol (HTTP, FTP, etc.) will be used
To encrypt the connection before any data is sent
To assign a dynamic port number to the client
questions.explain: The handshake establishes and synchronizes the connection state (SYN/SYN-ACK/ACK) for reliable delivery; it doesn't negotiate application protocols, provide encryption (that's TLS's job), or assign ports.

questions.q: Why is UDP generally faster than TCP for the same amount of data?
questions.correct: UDP has no acknowledgment/retransmission mechanism, allowing a continuous stream without waiting for ACKs
distractors: UDP packets are always physically smaller than TCP packets
UDP uses a different, faster physical network medium
UDP compresses data automatically before sending
questions.explain: The speed advantage comes from skipping TCP's ACK/windowing overhead, not from packet size, a different medium, or built-in compression, none of which UDP inherently provides.

questions.q: What is the primary purpose of NAT (Network Address Translation)?
questions.correct: To let devices using private, unregistered IP addresses communicate with the internet via a shared public address
distractors: To encrypt traffic leaving the private network
To load-balance traffic across multiple public IP addresses
To block unauthorized inbound connections, functioning as a firewall
questions.explain: NAT's core job is translating private addresses to a public one (and back) so internal hosts can reach the internet; it doesn't inherently encrypt traffic, load balance, or replace a firewall, though it can have a side effect of hiding internal hosts.

questions.q: What problem does the Spanning Tree Protocol (STP) solve at Layer 2?
questions.correct: It prevents network loops (and resulting broadcast storms) in redundant switch topologies
distractors: It assigns IP addresses to connected devices automatically
It load-balances traffic evenly across all redundant links simultaneously
questions.explain: STP blocks redundant paths to prevent loops/broadcast storms while keeping a backup path available; it doesn't handle encryption, IP assignment (that's DHCP), or simultaneous load-balancing across all links.

questions.q: Which command shows currently listening TCP ports specifically, using netstat?
questions.correct: netstat -atn
questions.explain: `-atn` filters for TCP listening/active sockets; `-aun` is the UDP equivalent, `-r` shows the routing table, and `-i` shows interface statistics.

questions.q: What does an SSH 'Host key verification failed' warning actually indicate?
questions.correct: The remote host's key doesn't match what your client previously stored, often because the server's host keys changed (e.g. after a reinstall)
distractors: Your SSH password was entered incorrectly
The remote server's firewall is blocking your connection
Your local system clock is out of sync with the server
questions.explain: This warning is specifically about a host identity mismatch versus your known_hosts record, not a password issue, firewall block, or clock skew (which would more likely affect Kerberos/certificate-based auth).

questions.q: Which command manually sends a raw HTTP GET request to a web server for debugging, using only a basic network utility?
questions.correct: telnet example.com 80 (followed by typing the raw HTTP request)
questions.explain: telnet can open a raw TCP connection on port 80 so you can type an HTTP request by hand; ping doesn't support a -p port flag for this purpose, and dig/traceroute aren't used to issue HTTP requests.

questions.q: Which command combination finds and forcefully kills whatever process is listening on port 80?
questions.correct: kill -9 $(lsof -t -i:80)
questions.explain: `lsof -t -i:80` outputs just the PID(s) on port 80, which kill -9 can then target; netstat -r shows routes (no PIDs), fuser -l lists signal names rather than killing, and ss -l alone doesn't extract PIDs directly for kill.

questions.q: You get `curl: (56) TCP connection reset by peer`. Which of these is a genuinely useful first troubleshooting step?
questions.correct: Verify the domain resolves to the correct IP address and double-check the URL scheme (http vs https) and Host header
distractors: Immediately assume the server's disk is full
Reinstall curl, since error 56 always means a broken curl installation
Restart your local machine's network interface, since the problem is always client-side
questions.explain: Checking DNS resolution and request details is a legitimate, low-risk first step for a connection reset; the error doesn't specifically indicate disk space, a broken curl install, or a guaranteed client-side cause.

questions.q: Which iptables rule allows inbound TCP traffic from a specific source IP address?
questions.correct: iptables -A INPUT -p tcp -s XXX.XXX.XXX.XXX -j ACCEPT
questions.explain: INPUT with -s (source) and -j ACCEPT allows inbound traffic from that IP; OUTPUT governs outbound traffic (wrong chain for 'inbound'), and the other two examples explicitly drop/reject rather than accept.

questions.q: In OpenBSD's pf firewall, what construct lets you dynamically add or remove blocked IP addresses without reloading the whole ruleset?
questions.correct: A pf table (managed at runtime with pfctl -t <table> -T add/delete)
distractors: A cron job that rewrites pf.conf every minute
A separate pf.conf file per IP address
questions.explain: pf tables are designed specifically for efficient, dynamic IP list management via pfctl; the other approaches are far clunkier or belong to a different tool (hosts.deny is TCP wrappers, not pf).

questions.q: When does Apache's access log typically record a request?
questions.correct: After the request has been completed
distractors: Before the request is received, as a prediction
Only when the request results in an error
Only for requests larger than a configured size threshold
questions.explain: Apache logs completed requests, not predicted or pre-emptive ones; it logs both successful and error requests (not errors only), and there's no default size-based logging cutoff.

questions.q: Why is it considered bad practice for a developer to use their own personal private SSH key on a server to deploy an application?
questions.correct: It ties deployment access to one individual's personal credential, which is a security and continuity risk if that person leaves or the key leaks
distractors: Private keys can only be used once and then must be regenerated
Private keys don't work over SSH for automated deployments at all
It violates SSH protocol rules and simply won't function
questions.explain: The real issue is operational/security risk (personal key tied to deploy access), not a technical limitation - private keys work fine for deploys and aren't single-use or protocol-violating.

questions.q: What does CORS actually do, in contrast to a Content Security Policy (CSP)?
questions.correct: CORS selectively relaxes the browser's Same-Origin Policy to allow specific cross-origin requests
distractors: CORS encrypts all cross-origin traffic between browser and server
CORS is a server-side firewall rule set, unrelated to browsers
CORS and CSP are two names for exactly the same browser security feature
questions.explain: CORS is specifically about relaxing same-origin restrictions for legitimate cross-origin requests; it's a browser-enforced HTTP header mechanism, not encryption, a firewall, or identical to CSP (which restricts what content sources a page may load).

questions.q: In nmap scan results, what does a 'filtered' port status mean?
questions.correct: nmap could not determine whether the port is open or closed, typically because a firewall is blocking the probe
distractors: The port is confirmed open but currently unused
The port is confirmed closed and will never respond
The port belongs to a deprecated protocol
questions.explain: 'Filtered' specifically reflects uncertainty caused by a firewall dropping/blocking probes, unlike a confirmed open or closed determination.

questions.q: What does tcpdump do to a network interface in order to capture all passing traffic, not just traffic addressed to the local host?
questions.correct: It puts the interface into promiscuous mode
distractors: It disables the interface's IP address temporarily
It converts the interface to a virtual bridge
It forces the interface into half-duplex mode
questions.explain: Promiscuous mode makes the NIC accept all packets it sees, not just ones addressed to it, which is what lets tcpdump capture broader traffic; the other changes aren't what enables packet capture.

questions.q: In Ansible, what are 'playbooks'?
questions.correct: Human-readable files, written in a text language, that describe configuration/deployment/orchestration steps for remote systems
distractors: Compiled binaries that execute configuration changes directly on the Ansible control node
A GUI-only feature for visually designing infrastructure diagrams
A database of previously executed shell commands
questions.explain: Playbooks are Ansible's core automation language, human-readable and declarative, not compiled binaries, a GUI feature, or a command history log.

questions.q: What is the purpose of NRPE (Nagios Remote Plugin Executor)?
questions.correct: It lets Nagios execute plugins on remote machines to monitor local resources like CPU and memory that aren't otherwise exposed
distractors: It replaces the need for Nagios plugins entirely with a built-in scanner
It encrypts all Nagios web dashboard traffic
It automatically restarts failed services on the remote machine
questions.explain: NRPE is an agent that runs Nagios plugin checks locally on the remote host and reports back; it doesn't replace plugins, handle dashboard encryption, or auto-restart services.

questions.q: In Nagios, what is the key difference between an active check and a passive check?
questions.correct: Active checks are initiated and performed by Nagios itself, while passive checks are submitted to Nagios by an external application
distractors: Active checks only work over HTTPS, passive checks only work over HTTP
Passive checks are always faster than active checks
Active checks can only monitor CPU, while passive checks monitor everything else
questions.explain: The defining difference is who initiates the check (Nagios vs. an external app); it has nothing to do with protocol, guaranteed speed, or which metrics can be monitored.

questions.q: Which git clone option ensures submodules are cloned along with the main repository?
questions.correct: --recurse-submodules
questions.explain: `--recurse-submodules` fetches submodule content along with the parent repo; `--depth 1` limits history depth, `--bare` creates a repo with no working directory, and `--mirror` clones all refs but isn't specifically for submodules.

questions.q: Which is a genuine advantage of Redis commonly cited by sysadmins?
questions.correct: Very high speed combined with support for rich data types like hashes, sets, and bitmaps
distractors: It requires no server-side locking mechanism whatsoever
It only supports simple string key-value pairs, nothing more complex
It cannot be accessed from the command line, only via application code
questions.explain: Redis is prized for speed and rich data structures (and does support server-side locking); it isn't limited to plain strings, and `redis-cli` provides direct command-line access.

questions.q: What is Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) fundamentally caused by?
questions.correct: Untrusted, unvalidated user input being processed and executed as script on the client side
distractors: A server misconfiguration that exposes the database directly to the internet
Weak password hashing algorithms on the login page
A firewall rule allowing too many open ports
questions.explain: XSS specifically arises from unvalidated input being rendered/executed as script client-side; it isn't about database exposure, password hashing, or firewall port rules.

questions.q: Why might an enterprise prefer a NIDS (Network Intrusion Detection System) over a HIDS (Host Intrusion Detection System) at scale?
questions.correct: NIDS is centrally placed on the network and easier to manage than deploying and maintaining HIDS on every individual host
distractors: NIDS can see encrypted payload contents that HIDS cannot
HIDS only works on Windows servers, never Linux
NIDS consumes more host CPU resources than HIDS
questions.explain: NIDS's central network placement is easier to manage at scale compared to per-host HIDS deployment/maintenance; it doesn't inherently see through encryption better, and HIDS is OS-agnostic, and NIDS runs on dedicated network gear rather than consuming host CPU.

questions.q: What does 'compliance' mean in a cybersecurity/IT context?
questions.correct: Adhering to a set of standards defined by a government, industry body, or independent organization, such as PCI DSS for payment data
distractors: Having zero security vulnerabilities in your systems
Using only open-source software throughout your infrastructure
Passing a single one-time security audit, with no ongoing requirement
questions.explain: Compliance is about ongoing adherence to defined standards (like PCI DSS), not a claim of zero vulnerabilities, a software licensing choice, or a one-time audit event.

questions.q: What is the core function of a Web Application Firewall (WAF)?
questions.correct: It filters legitimate web traffic from malicious traffic to protect an application
distractors: It encrypts all traffic between the database and application server
It replaces the need for TLS certificates on the web server
It only protects against DDoS attacks, nothing else
questions.explain: A WAF's job is filtering application-layer traffic for malicious patterns; it doesn't handle database encryption, replace TLS, or limit itself to DDoS mitigation.

questions.q: What was a major drawback of the original monolithic kernel architecture?
questions.correct: Large kernel size and poor maintainability, since bug fixes or new features required rebuilding much of the kernel
distractors: It could not run more than one process at a time
It required proprietary hardware to function at all
It had no support for interrupt handling whatsoever
questions.explain: The monolithic design's problems were size and maintainability due to everything being packaged into one module; it wasn't limited to single-process execution, proprietary hardware, or lacking interrupts.

questions.q: A program fails with a missing library error. Which environment variable lets you point it to a nonstandard library location, searched before the standard directories?
questions.correct: LD_LIBRARY_PATH
questions.explain: LD_LIBRARY_PATH specifically controls the dynamic linker's search path at runtime; PATH is for executables (not libraries), LD_PRELOAD forces specific libraries to load first (not a search path), and LIBRARY_PATH is used at compile/link time, not runtime.

questions.q: What is a key reason to synchronize UID/GID values across multiple systems on a network?
questions.correct: So the same username/UID maps consistently to the same person across all systems, simplifying access management and permissions on shared resources (e.g. NFS)
distractors: It is required for TCP/IP to function between hosts
It automatically encrypts all user home directories
It removes the need for a centralized authentication system like LDAP
questions.explain: Consistent UID/GID mapping mainly matters for permission consistency (especially over shared filesystems); it isn't required for basic TCP/IP, doesn't provide encryption, and doesn't replace centralized auth - it often works alongside it.

questions.q: In BSD systems, which file is the primary startup configuration file that /etc/rc and /etc/rc.d scripts include?
questions.correct: /etc/defaults/rc.conf
questions.explain: BSD's startup scripts include /etc/defaults/rc.conf (with actual customizations placed in /etc/rc.conf); inittab and systemd files are Linux-specific init mechanisms, and rc.local is also a Linux convention, not the BSD primary config.

questions.q: Which Linux system call is used specifically to create a new process?
questions.correct: fork()
questions.explain: fork() creates a new (child) process; exec() replaces a process's image with a new program, wait() blocks until a child changes state, and getpid() just returns the current process ID.

questions.q: Within a POSIX inode, which field records how many hard links point to that inode?
questions.correct: The link count
questions.explain: The link count specifically tracks the number of hard links; device ID identifies the containing device, file mode covers type/permissions, and the serial number (inode number itself) is a separate identifier.

questions.q: Is the fact that ordinary users can read /etc/passwd a security hole on modern Linux systems?
questions.correct: No, because the actual password hashes are stored separately in /etc/shadow, which ordinary users cannot read
distractors: Yes, because /etc/passwd still contains readable plaintext passwords by default
Yes, but only on systems that don't use PAM
No, because /etc/passwd is encrypted at rest automatically
questions.explain: Modern systems shadow the password hashes into /etc/shadow (root-readable only), so /etc/passwd being world-readable is not a hole; it's not about PAM specifically, and /etc/passwd isn't encrypted, just no longer holding the sensitive hash.

questions.q: Which command lets you run an action every time a specific file is modified, by watching filesystem events?
questions.correct: inotifywait
questions.explain: inotifywait blocks until a filesystem event (like close_write) occurs, making it suitable for event-driven triggers; `watch` just re-runs a command on a timer, `crontab` schedules by time, and `at` runs a one-off job at a specific time - none of these are event-driven on file changes.

questions.q: Which of these is a commonly cited risk/caveat of using LVM (Logical Volume Management)?
questions.correct: Its more complex on-disk structures can make data recovery harder if something goes wrong
distractors: It cannot be resized after creation under any circumstances
It is incompatible with all modern Linux filesystems
It doubles the required physical disk space for any volume
questions.explain: The real risk cited is recovery difficulty due to complexity (plus snapshot fragility); LVM volumes actually can be resized, are broadly filesystem-compatible, and don't inherently double space requirements.

questions.q: Is there any process that even root's `kill -9` cannot terminate?
questions.correct: Yes - PID 1 (the init process) cannot be killed with a fatal signal, even by root
distractors: No, kill -9 as root can always terminate any process instantly with zero exceptions
Yes - any process owned by a non-root user is immune to root's kill -9
Yes - any setuid process is completely immune to SIGKILL
questions.explain: PID 1 is specifically protected from fatal signals as a kernel design choice; ordinary non-root-owned and setuid processes are not immune to root's SIGKILL, and delivery of SIGKILL is not instantaneous/synchronous even when it does apply.

questions.q: What is the key difference between `disown` and `nohup` for a background job?
questions.correct: disown removes a job from the shell's job control table (so the shell won't SIGHUP it) but the process stays connected to the terminal, while nohup makes the process itself ignore SIGHUP
distractors: disown and nohup are two names for the exact same functionality
nohup only works on jobs already running in the background, while disown works on any command
disown redirects a process's output to /dev/null automatically, while nohup does not
questions.explain: disown affects the shell's tracking of the job (not the process's own signal handling), while nohup changes how the process itself responds to SIGHUP; they aren't identical, and it's nohup (not disown) that's typically launched before/with a command, while disown targets already-backgrounded jobs.

questions.q: What is a key advantage of running a process inside a chroot environment?
questions.correct: The process's filesystem view is isolated from the actual host filesystem, using a different directory as its apparent root
distractors: It automatically encrypts all files the process creates
It gives the process full root privileges regardless of its actual user
It removes the need to mount /dev, /proc, or /sys inside the jail
questions.explain: chroot's core benefit is filesystem isolation via a new apparent root directory; it doesn't grant privileges, encrypt data, or eliminate the need to bind-mount special filesystems like /dev, /proc, /sys inside the jail for many programs to function correctly.

questions.q: What causes a segmentation fault (segfault)?
questions.correct: A program attempting to read or write to a memory location it isn't allowed to access
distractors: A program running out of CPU time allotted by the scheduler
A network connection timing out during a system call
A disk write operation failing due to a full filesystem
questions.explain: Segfaults are specifically about illegal memory access, not CPU scheduling, network timeouts, or disk space issues (though those can cause other kinds of errors).

questions.q: For generating random passwords, which source of entropy is generally recommended over the alternative?
questions.correct: /dev/urandom, over /dev/random
questions.explain: /dev/urandom is the recommended source for practical cryptographic randomness (non-blocking, effectively secure); /dev/random can block waiting for entropy, and /dev/zero/dev/null don't provide randomness at all.

questions.q: What happens to a user whose login shell is set to /bin/false?
questions.correct: They are immediately logged out, since /bin/false exits immediately upon being called
distractors: They see a polite custom message before being denied access
They are given a restricted shell with read-only access
They are granted a normal shell but with no home directory
questions.explain: /bin/false just exits immediately with no message, causing an instant logout; the polite custom message behavior described is characteristic of /sbin/nologin instead.

questions.q: In FreeBSD, what does the error 'maxproc limit exceeded by uid' typically indicate, and what kernel variable controls it?
questions.correct: Too many processes for that user/system; controlled by the kern.maxusers variable
distractors: A corrupted user database requiring a full reinstall
A licensing limit imposed by the FreeBSD Foundation
A hardware failure in the process scheduler
questions.explain: This is a resource-limit message tied to kern.maxusers (which scales several kernel limits including max processes); it's not related to licensing, hardware failure, or database corruption.

questions.q: When reading a file line by line in bash with a while loop, why is `IFS=''` commonly used before `read -r line`?
questions.correct: To prevent leading/trailing whitespace on each line from being trimmed
distractors: To make the loop run in a background subshell
To automatically convert tabs into spaces
To disable comment parsing within the file
questions.explain: IFS='' preserves whitespace that read would otherwise strip; it has no effect on subshelling, tab conversion, or comment handling.

questions.q: A server shows a load average above 30 on 24 cores, yet CPU is around 70% idle. What is a common cause of this pattern?
questions.correct: High I/O wait - processes are blocked waiting on disk reads/writes, inflating load average without high CPU usage
distractors: The load average calculation is simply broken on multi-core systems
Network latency to a remote DNS server is always the cause
Too many zombie processes are consuming load average slots
questions.explain: Processes stuck in uninterruptible I/O wait count toward load average without using CPU, which explains high load with idle CPU; it's not a broken calculation, and zombies (already-terminated processes) don't inflate load average this way.

questions.q: Which SSH client option combination forces login using password authentication only, disabling public key auth for that connection?
questions.correct: -o PreferredAuthentications=password -o PubkeyAuthentication=no
questions.explain: Setting PreferredAuthentications to password and explicitly disabling PubkeyAuthentication forces password-only login; the other combinations either force key-based auth or don't disable key auth at all.

questions.q: PostgreSQL is throwing 'Too many open files' errors. Which config parameter, found in postgresql.conf, directly controls this per subprocess?
questions.correct: max_files_per_process
questions.explain: max_files_per_process directly caps simultaneously open files per server subprocess; shared_buffers controls memory caching, max_connections limits concurrent client connections, and work_mem controls per-query memory - none directly cap open file handles.

questions.q: `df` and `du` sometimes disagree about available disk space. What is a classic cause of this?
questions.correct: A file is deleted but still held open by a running process, so `du` no longer counts it but `df` still shows the space as used
distractors: `du` always rounds up file sizes, while `df` always rounds down
`df` only works on ext4 filesystems, causing mismatches elsewhere
`du` counts inodes while `df` counts blocks, so they're never expected to match
questions.explain: The classic explanation is deleted-but-open files still consuming disk space that `df` reports but `du` (which walks the directory tree) can no longer see; it's not a rounding quirk, filesystem restriction, or a simple unit mismatch.

questions.q: What is the fundamental difference between hashing and encryption?
questions.correct: Encryption is reversible (can be decrypted back to the original), while hashing produces an irreversible, fixed-length digest
distractors: Hashing is reversible while encryption is not
Both are equally reversible, differing only in key length
Hashing always produces a longer output than encryption
questions.explain: Encryption is a two-way process (encrypt/decrypt with a key), whereas a hash is designed to be a one-way, irreversible condensation of data - the reverse of the incorrect option given.

questions.q: Should a self-signed root certificate be included in a web server's SSL certificate chain configuration?
questions.correct: No - clients ignore it anyway, and including it only adds unnecessary size/latency to the handshake
distractors: Yes - without it, clients can never establish a TLS connection
Yes - it's required for the intermediate certificate to be considered valid
No - including it will cause the TLS handshake to fail immediately
questions.explain: Root certificates are meant to already exist in the client's trust store; sending it just adds handshake overhead without helping trust, but it also doesn't outright break the handshake, and it's not required for the intermediate cert's validity.

questions.q: Which tool is the standard way to log every command executed by root (euid=0) on a production server?
questions.correct: auditd, using execve syscall rules in /etc/audit/audit.rules
distractors: syslog-ng, using a custom root-only facility
logrotate, with a dedicated root job
cron, with a per-minute logging script
questions.explain: auditd with execve syscall rules filtered on euid=0 is the standard mechanism for this; syslog-ng and logrotate handle general/rotating logs (not syscall-level auditing), and cron isn't suited to real-time command auditing.

questions.q: Which technique helps prevent a large `dd` operation from freezing the whole system due to disk I/O contention?
questions.correct: Running dd with a reduced I/O priority using ionice (e.g. ionice -c3)
distractors: Running dd with the highest possible nice value for CPU priority only
Piping dd's output through gzip to reduce total data written
Running dd as a background job with disown
questions.explain: ionice specifically controls disk I/O scheduling priority, directly addressing I/O contention; nice affects CPU scheduling (not disk I/O), compressing output changes data size but not I/O priority, and disown only affects shell job control, not I/O behavior.

questions.q: Which tool applies a CPU usage limit to a whole group/set of processes at once, rather than just one process?
questions.correct: cgroups
questions.explain: cgroups can constrain resources for a group of processes collectively; nice/renice adjust scheduling priority for individual processes, and cpulimit throttles one specific running process.

questions.q: Which command-line tool throttles a single already-running process to a specific percentage of CPU, e.g. capping it at 50%?
questions.correct: cpulimit -l 50 COMMAND
questions.explain: cpulimit's `-l` flag takes an actual percentage cap; nice/renice only adjust scheduling priority (not a hard percentage), and ionice controls disk I/O priority, not CPU.

questions.q: Which command mounts a RAM-backed temporary filesystem of 64MB at /mnt?
questions.correct: mount -t tmpfs tmpfs /mnt -o size=64M
questions.explain: tmpfs is the standard RAM-backed filesystem type for this purpose; ext4/proc/swap are not appropriate filesystem types for mounting an ad hoc RAM disk this way.

questions.q: Which command forcefully kills whatever process currently holds a lock on a specific file?
questions.correct: fuser -k filename
questions.explain: `fuser -k` identifies and kills processes using a given file; `kill` requires a PID (not a filename), `lsof` doesn't have a `-k` kill option, and `chattr` changes file attributes, not process state.

questions.q: If someone accidentally runs `chmod -x /bin/chmod`, removing chmod's own execute permission, which approach can restore it without a working chmod binary?
questions.correct: Use a statically-linked alternative like busybox's chmod, or setfacl, to restore permissions
distractors: Simply run `chmod +x /bin/chmod` again from the same shell
Reboot the system, which automatically resets binary permissions
Edit /etc/passwd to grant yourself temporary execute rights
questions.explain: Since chmod itself lost execute permission, you can't just re-run chmod - you need an alternative tool like busybox chmod or setfacl instead; a reboot won't reset binary permissions, and /etc/passwd controls user accounts, not file permission bits.

questions.q: What is the key difference between GRUB's `grub>` and `grub-rescue>` prompts?
questions.correct: grub-rescue appears when GRUB cannot even find its own directory/configuration, offering far fewer commands than the full grub> mode
distractors: grub> is only accessible in UEFI mode, while grub-rescue is BIOS-only
grub-rescue is simply a renamed alias for grub> with identical functionality
grub> only appears after a successful OS boot, not before it
questions.explain: grub-rescue is a stripped-down fallback mode reached when GRUB can't locate its normal directory/config, offering minimal commands; it isn't UEFI/BIOS-specific, isn't identical to grub>, and grub> is reached before boot completes, from the boot menu.

questions.q: Which command checks whether an SSL private key and certificate match, by comparing their moduli?
questions.correct: Comparing MD5 hashes of `openssl rsa -noout -modulus` and `openssl x509 -noout -modulus` output
questions.explain: Comparing hashed moduli from the key and cert is the standard technique; `openssl verify` checks trust chains (not key/cert matching this way), a raw `diff` won't work since the files are structurally different, and there's no such `-check-key` flag.

questions.q: Which utility should be used with `vipw` to safely add a new user entry directly into /etc/passwd without useradd/adduser?
questions.correct: vipw itself, which locks the file to prevent concurrent updates
