distractors: A plain text editor like vim opened directly on /etc/passwd
cp to overwrite /etc/passwd with a new version
questions.explain: vipw specifically locks /etc/passwd during editing to prevent races with other tools; editing directly with vim/sed or overwriting with cp risks corruption from concurrent access.

questions.q: Why is `mktemp` preferred over manually constructing a temporary filename in a root-running script?
questions.correct: mktemp randomizes the filename, preventing an attacker from pre-creating a symlink at a predictable path to hijack the write
distractors: mktemp automatically encrypts the temporary file's contents
mktemp guarantees the file will be deleted after the script exits
mktemp is required by POSIX and manual filenames will cause a syntax error
questions.explain: The real security benefit is unpredictability, defeating symlink-based attacks on predictable temp paths; mktemp doesn't encrypt content, doesn't auto-delete the file, and manual filenames are syntactically valid, just insecure.

questions.q: Why can attaching `strace` to a production process be risky?
questions.correct: strace uses ptrace(), which pauses the target process on every syscall entry and exit, potentially causing serious slowdowns
distractors: strace permanently modifies the binary being traced
strace requires the target process to be restarted first
strace only works on processes not currently accepting network connections
questions.explain: ptrace-based tracing pauses the process twice per syscall, which can meaningfully degrade performance on a busy production process; it doesn't modify the binary, doesn't require a restart, and works fine on processes handling network connections.

questions.q: What is the most portable, safest way to delete a file literally named `-rf`?
questions.correct: rm ./-fr
questions.explain: Prefixing with `./` prevents the shell/rm from interpreting the filename as flags; plain `rm -rf` would be parsed as options rather than a filename, and the other variants either don't solve the parsing issue or aren't portable escaping methods.

questions.q: What is the purpose of adding a 'salt' when hashing a password for storage in /etc/shadow?
questions.correct: To defend against dictionary and precomputed (rainbow table) attacks by making each hash unique even for identical passwords
distractors: To make the password hash reversible back to plaintext when needed
To compress the password hash to a smaller storage size
To allow the same hash to work across multiple different user accounts
questions.explain: Salting defeats precomputed/dictionary attacks by ensuring identical passwords produce different hashes; it doesn't make hashing reversible, doesn't compress anything, and each user's hash remains unique to their account.

questions.q: Which tag must always begin a valid SPF (Sender Policy Framework) DNS record?
questions.correct: v=spf1
questions.explain: SPF records must start with the v=spf1 version tag; DKIM and DMARC are separate, related but distinct email authentication mechanisms with their own record formats.

questions.q: What distinguishes an authoritative DNS answer from a nonauthoritative one?
questions.correct: An authoritative answer comes directly from the name server hosting the domain's actual zone files; a nonauthoritative answer comes from a server that only has it cached
distractors: Authoritative answers are always faster than nonauthoritative ones
Nonauthoritative answers are always wrong or outdated
Authoritative answers can only come from root DNS servers
questions.explain: The distinction is about the source (zone-file-hosting server vs. a caching resolver), not speed, correctness, or being limited to root servers - domain-specific authoritative servers, not just root servers, give authoritative answers.

questions.q: If resolv.conf lists two nameservers but only the second one actually has a record, and the resolver still returns NXDOMAIN, what is the likely reason?
questions.correct: The resolver only moves on to the second nameserver if the first one times out - if the first nameserver responds (even with NXDOMAIN), the resolver won't try the second one
distractors: resolv.conf can only ever use the first nameserver listed, ignoring the second entirely
NXDOMAIN always means both nameservers are completely offline
The resolver load-balances randomly between the two nameservers on every query
questions.explain: Standard resolver behavior only falls back to the next server on timeout, not on a valid (even negative) response from the first, which explains the NXDOMAIN despite the second server having the record.

questions.q: Can an SSL certificate be issued for a public IP address instead of a domain name?
questions.correct: Yes, though it's uncommon - the IP can be specified as the Common Name in the CSR
distractors: No, SSL certificates can only ever be issued for FQDNs
Yes, but only for private/internal (RFC1918) IP addresses
No, this was possible in SSL but was removed entirely in TLS
questions.explain: IP-based certificates are valid (if rare) for public IPs specifically; it's not restricted to private IPs, isn't impossible, and wasn't removed when TLS superseded SSL.

questions.q: Does putting Varnish in front of your web app automatically solve load balancing and redundancy needs?
questions.correct: No - a single Varnish instance can itself become a single point of failure, even though Varnish can be configured to load-balance across backend servers
distractors: Yes - Varnish inherently provides full redundancy with zero additional configuration
No - Varnish cannot perform any load-balancing function at all
Yes - Varnish replaces the need for multiple web servers entirely
questions.explain: A lone Varnish instance is itself a potential single point of failure unless made redundant, even though it can be configured for load-balancing; it doesn't eliminate the need for multiple backend servers or provide automatic redundancy.

questions.q: In Varnish Cache terminology, what is a 'hit-for-pass'?
questions.correct: A case where Varnish determines a requested object is uncacheable and will simply pass the request through rather than caching it
distractors: A request successfully served entirely from cache
A request that finds nothing in cache and must fetch from the origin server
A request that is deliberately blocked by a Varnish security rule
questions.explain: Hit-for-pass specifically marks content as uncacheable so future requests skip caching attempts; a normal cache hit is fully served from cache, and a miss just means the cache was empty (not that content is uncacheable).

questions.q: .htaccess files were originally designed to solve which problem?
questions.correct: Letting shared-hosting sysadmins allow multiple clients to customize Apache behavior for their own site without granting access to the full server config
distractors: Providing faster page load times than server-level configuration
Replacing the need for a firewall on shared hosting servers
Encrypting website traffic without needing an SSL certificate
questions.explain: .htaccess exists to give per-directory config control to clients without full server access, historically for shared hosting; it isn't about speed, firewalling, or encryption.

questions.q: What is SNI (Server Name Indication) primarily used for in an SSL/TLS connection?
questions.correct: It lets a client indicate which hostname it's trying to reach during the TLS handshake, allowing multiple SSL certificates to be served from a single IP address
distractors: It encrypts the initial TCP handshake before TLS negotiation begins
It replaces the need for a certificate authority entirely
It only applies to email protocols like SMTPS, not HTTPS
questions.explain: SNI's core purpose is multiplexing several domains/certificates on one IP by telling the server which hostname is requested up front; it doesn't encrypt the TCP handshake itself, doesn't remove the need for CAs, and applies broadly to TLS, including HTTPS.

questions.q: How does a browser set a cookie on the client via HTTP?
questions.correct: The server sends a Set-Cookie header in its response, and the browser echoes it back with a Cookie header on subsequent requests
distractors: The browser generates cookies locally with no server involvement at all
Cookies are set exclusively via JavaScript, never via HTTP headers
The client sends a Set-Cookie header first, which the server then must approve
questions.explain: The standard flow is server sends Set-Cookie, client later sends Cookie; cookies can also be set via JavaScript, but the classic HTTP mechanism is server-initiated, not client-initiated or JS-exclusive.

questions.q: Why do POST request parameters sometimes get lost when a server issues an HTTP redirect to an external API?
questions.correct: HTTP redirects (3xx responses) never resend POST body data - clients that do so are violating the HTTP spec
distractors: POST parameters are only preserved if sent over HTTPS
Redirects strip query string parameters but always preserve POST bodies
This only happens with Nginx specifically, never with Apache
questions.explain: Per the HTTP spec, redirects don't carry POST body data forward; this isn't about the HTTP vs HTTPS scheme, doesn't only affect query strings while preserving bodies, and isn't specific to one particular web server.

questions.q: What is the recommended way to benchmark NFS performance realistically?
questions.correct: Test with the actual application workload you normally run against it, since load patterns vary drastically by use case
distractors: Only use a single synthetic tool like bonnie++ and trust its result universally
NFS performance is identical regardless of workload, so any benchmark works
Rely solely on the NFS server's default logging output
questions.explain: Real workload testing matters because NFS load patterns (compiling code vs. simple logins vs. web home directories) differ significantly; a single synthetic benchmark, assuming uniform performance, or relying only on logs won't capture that variability.

questions.q: When blocking many IPs from the same subnet, why might a null (black-hole) route be more efficient than adding equivalent iptables rules?
questions.correct: On systems with a small routing table, adding a null route can be processed more efficiently than growing an already extensive iptables rule set
distractors: Null routes work at a completely different layer that bypasses the kernel entirely
iptables cannot block ranges of IP addresses under any circumstances
Null routes automatically update themselves without any admin configuration
questions.explain: The efficiency argument is about traversal cost given the existing rule set/routing table size; iptables can absolutely block CIDR ranges, and null routes don't self-configure or bypass the kernel.

questions.q: Which approach lets you copy a file directly between two remote hosts, without downloading it to your local machine first?
questions.correct: Chaining SSH commands, e.g. ssh user1@remote1 'ssh user2@remote2 "cat file"' > file
distractors: scp remote1:file remote2:file run from your local machine only
rsync -a remote1:file remote2:file with no SSH access to either host
questions.explain: Nesting SSH sessions (or an SSH tunnel) lets data flow directly between the two remote hosts; plain scp/rsync syntax as shown still requires proper SSH access configured between hosts, and wget doesn't perform host-to-host transfers this way.

questions.q: Which caching layer is checked FIRST when you type a URL into a browser and press enter?
questions.correct: The browser's own internal DNS cache
questions.explain: The lookup chain starts with the browser's own cache, then falls back to the OS resolver cache, then external DNS servers, and finally the authoritative server, in roughly that order.

questions.q: What is the key difference between `Cache-Control: max-age=0` and `Cache-Control: no-cache`?
questions.correct: max-age=0 marks the response as immediately stale but allows caches to use it under certain conditions, while no-cache requires revalidation before any use
distractors: They are functionally identical directives with different names
max-age=0 completely disables caching, while no-cache allows unlimited caching
no-cache prevents the browser from storing the response at all, while max-age=0 allows storage
questions.explain: no-cache is the stricter directive, mandating revalidation before use, while max-age=0 is more of a 'treat this as stale' hint; they aren't identical, and no-cache doesn't mean 'not stored' (that would be 'no-store').

questions.q: What security risk does setting `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` introduce?
questions.correct: It allows any website to make cross-origin requests to your site and read the response, potentially exposing data meant only for trusted origins
distractors: It exposes your server's private SSH keys to the public internet
It disables HTTPS enforcement on the affected endpoint
It only affects requests made from within the same origin, so there's no real risk
questions.explain: The wildcard CORS header opens your responses to any origin's cross-site requests, which is the actual risk; it has nothing to do with SSH keys or HTTPS enforcement, and the risk is specifically about cross-origin (not same-origin) requests.

questions.q: Which nmap technique spoofs packets to appear as if they're coming from multiple other hosts, to make firewall log analysis harder for defenders?
questions.correct: Decoy scanning (nmap -D)
questions.explain: Decoy scanning (-D) specifically generates spoofed source addresses alongside the real one in firewall logs; the other listed nmap techniques serve different evasion/detection purposes and don't work by injecting multiple fake source IPs into logs the same way.

questions.q: In Nagios, what condition is described as 'flapping'?
questions.correct: A host or service changing state too frequently, generating repeated recovery/problem notifications
distractors: A host that has been down for more than 24 hours continuously
A service that consistently reports the same state without ever changing
A configuration file failing to load on Nagios startup
questions.explain: Flapping specifically refers to rapid, repeated state changes causing notification noise; it's not about prolonged downtime, static state, or config load failures.

questions.q: Which of these is a genuine advantage containers have over traditional virtual machines?
questions.correct: Faster, lighter-weight provisioning with better resource utilization
distractors: Containers provide stronger kernel-level isolation than VMs
Containers require their own full guest operating system per instance
VMs always start faster than containers due to lower overhead
questions.explain: Containers are lighter and provision faster with efficient resource use; VMs, not containers, run a full separate guest OS each, and VMs are generally slower to provision, plus containers typically share the host kernel, so isolation is generally considered weaker than a VM's, not stronger.

questions.q: Which is a common legitimate use case for LXC/LXD containers?
questions.correct: Testing an application against multiple different Linux distributions or software versions in isolation
distractors: Running fully separate kernels for each isolated environment
Replacing the need for any configuration management tooling
Providing hardware-level virtualization identical to a hypervisor
questions.explain: LXC/LXD is well suited to isolated testing across distros/versions on a shared kernel; containers share the host kernel (not separate kernels each), don't inherently replace config management, and aren't the same as hardware-level hypervisor virtualization.

questions.q: Which of these is a recommended security measure when preparing a Redis cluster?
questions.correct: Binding Redis to 127.0.0.1 (or firewalling it) and enabling AUTH/Protected Mode if external access isn't required
distractors: Leaving Redis's default port open to all interfaces for easier debugging
Disabling all authentication to simplify client connections
Running Redis as the root user to avoid permission errors
questions.explain: Restricting network exposure and enabling AUTH/Protected Mode are genuine Redis hardening steps; leaving it open, disabling auth, or running as root are all the opposite of good security practice.

questions.q: What defines a Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) vulnerability?
questions.correct: The server processes a request without properly verifying that it genuinely originated from a trusted, authenticated client action
distractors: An attacker directly exploits a buffer overflow in the server's memory
An attacker steals credentials through a fake login page
An attacker floods the server with excessive traffic to cause denial of service
questions.explain: CSRF is specifically about a lack of origin/intent verification for requests, tricking an authenticated user's browser into submitting unwanted actions; it's unrelated to buffer overflows, phishing, or DoS flooding.

questions.q: In an organization's security documentation hierarchy, what is the role of a 'process' document, as distinct from a 'policy'?
questions.correct: A process gives detailed, step-by-step instructions for implementing a security mechanism, while a policy defines the higher-level objectives and framework
distractors: A process and a policy are interchangeable terms for the same document type
A policy is optional guidance, while a process is always legally mandated
A process only applies to IT staff, while policies apply to executives only
questions.explain: Policies set objectives/framework, processes detail exact implementation steps, and guidelines offer customizable recommendations - three distinct levels, not interchangeable, mandatory-vs-optional, or role-restricted documents.

questions.q: In IDS terminology, what is a 'false positive'?
questions.correct: The system raises an alert for an intrusion that did not actually happen
distractors: The system fails to alert on an intrusion that did actually happen
The system correctly identifies and blocks a real intrusion
The system crashes while processing legitimate traffic
questions.explain: A false positive is an alert with no real intrusion behind it; failing to alert on a real intrusion is instead a false negative, and a correct detection or a crash are different scenarios entirely.

questions.q: Which of these is a genuine web server hardening recommendation?
questions.correct: Mounting /tmp on a separate partition with nodev, nosuid, and noexec options set
distractors: Disabling all logging to reduce disk I/O overhead
Running all web server worker processes as root for simplicity
Combining /var, /var/log, and / into a single partition to save space
questions.explain: Isolating /tmp with restrictive mount options is a real hardening step; disabling logging removes forensic visibility, running as root violates least-privilege, and merging log partitions into / risks filling the root filesystem and losing separation of concerns.

questions.q: Which tool lets you run `top` in batch mode to periodically log a specific process's memory, thread count, and CPU usage for profiling?
questions.correct: top -b -p `pidof a.out`
questions.explain: top's `-b` (batch) mode combined with `-p` targeting a PID logs periodic snapshots suitable for profiling; the other options/flags as shown aren't real top/ps/htop mechanisms for this.

questions.q: On a minimal system without telnet available, which virtual filesystem path can you check to see if a network interface has a carrier (link) present?
questions.correct: /sys/class/net/<iface>/carrier
questions.explain: sysfs exposes per-interface link status at /sys/class/net/<iface>/carrier; the other paths given aren't real Linux virtual filesystem locations for this purpose.

questions.q: What is the 'principle of least privilege', cited as a golden rule for limiting the impact of a hacked system?
questions.correct: Configure each service to run as a user with only the minimum rights necessary to do its job, containing the blast radius of a compromise
distractors: Give every service root privileges so it can self-heal after an attack
Grant maximum privileges to the security team only, restricting everyone else equally
Disable all user accounts except one shared administrative account
questions.explain: Least privilege limits what a compromised service can do by minimizing its rights; it's the opposite of granting root broadly, isn't about restricting only non-security staff, and isn't about consolidating to one shared account.

questions.q: What does the shell fork bomb `:(){ :|:& };:` actually do?
questions.correct: It defines a function that recursively calls two copies of itself in the background, exponentially consuming process table entries and system resources
distractors: It permanently deletes all files in the current directory
It opens a reverse shell to a remote attacker-controlled host
It floods the network interface with malformed packets
questions.explain: This is a classic fork bomb - a self-referencing function spawning copies of itself exponentially; it doesn't delete files, open remote shells, or send network packets on its own.

questions.q: How can you recover the contents of a file that was deleted but is still held open by a running process like Apache?
questions.correct: Access it through the process's open file descriptor symlink under /proc/<pid>/fd/<fd>
distractors: Use `fsck` to rebuild the file from its inode after the fact
Simply reopen the file by its original filename, since Linux caches deleted names
Restore it from the filesystem's journal using `journalctl`
questions.explain: /proc/<pid>/fd/ exposes still-open file descriptors as accessible symlinks even after deletion; you cannot reopen a deleted file by its old name, fsck doesn't restore data this way, and journalctl is for systemd logs, not filesystem journaling recovery.

questions.q: To reinstall a Linux system on a server with no out-of-band management console access, while it's still running another Linux OS, which tool is used to bootstrap the new root filesystem?
questions.correct: debootstrap
distractors: dd, imaging the disk directly with no working directory
apt-get install --reinstall on the running system
fdisk, to repartition the running root filesystem live
questions.explain: debootstrap builds a minimal new Debian-based root filesystem into a working directory that can later be chrooted into and made bootable; dd imaging, reinstalling packages on the live OS, or live repartitioning the active root don't achieve an in-place OS replacement this way.

questions.q: After rsync's OOM killer event, which file controls whether processes are allowed to request more memory than is actually free on the system?
questions.correct: /proc/sys/vm/overcommit_memory
questions.explain: overcommit_memory governs whether the kernel allows requests exceeding currently free memory (enabling the OOM killer scenario); swappiness affects swap usage tendency, kernel.panic controls reboot-on-panic behavior, and dirty_ratio governs writeback thresholds - all different tunables.

questions.q: What determines which process the Linux OOM killer chooses to terminate first when memory is exhausted?
questions.correct: The process with the highest oom_score, reflecting how much memory would be freed versus how important the process is judged to be
distractors: Strictly the process that has been running the longest
Strictly the process consuming the least memory, to finish it off quickly
A purely random selection among all running processes
questions.explain: The OOM killer ranks processes by oom_score to balance freeing significant memory against killing the least critical process; it isn't based purely on process age, isn't targeting the smallest memory consumer, and isn't random.

questions.q: Which DNS record type is used to route email to the correct mail server for a domain?
questions.correct: MX record
questions.explain: MX records specify mail exchange servers and priority; CNAME is a name alias, A maps to an IPv4 address, and SOA holds authoritative zone metadata, none of which route mail directly.

questions.q: Which DNS record type creates an alias pointing one domain name to another domain name (rather than to an IP)?
questions.correct: CNAME record
questions.explain: CNAME aliases one name to another name; A records map directly to an IPv4 address, PTR does reverse IP-to-name lookups, and MX is specifically for mail routing.

questions.q: Which DNS record holds the authoritative information about a zone, including the primary name server and refresh timers?
questions.correct: SOA (Start of Authority) record
questions.explain: SOA specifically holds zone authority metadata like serial number and refresh/retry timers; NS just lists name servers, A maps to an address, and TXT holds arbitrary text data.

questions.q: In HTTP status codes, what does the 2xx range indicate?
questions.correct: Success - the client's request was accepted and processed successfully
distractors: The client needs to take further action to complete the request
An error occurred that is the server's responsibility
questions.explain: 2xx codes signal success; 3xx codes are redirection (further action needed), 5xx are server errors, and 1xx are informational only.

questions.q: In HTTP status codes, what does the 5xx range indicate?
questions.correct: Server-side error - the server takes responsibility for failing to fulfill a valid request
distractors: Client-side error, where the client is at fault
A redirection requiring further client action
questions.explain: 5xx specifically means the server itself failed to fulfill a valid request; 4xx (not 5xx) points to client-side errors, 3xx is redirection, and 2xx is success.

questions.q: Which Linux syscall replaces a running process's memory image with a new program, without creating a new process?
questions.correct: exec()
questions.explain: exec() replaces the current process image in place; fork() creates a brand-new child process instead, wait() blocks for a child's state change, and getppid() just retrieves the parent PID.

questions.q: Which Linux syscall makes a parent process pause until one of its child processes changes state (e.g. exits)?
questions.correct: wait()
questions.explain: wait() specifically blocks the calling process until a child's state changes; fork() creates children, exec() replaces a process image, and nice() adjusts scheduling priority.

questions.q: Which Linux syscall adjusts a process's scheduling priority (niceness)?
questions.correct: nice()
questions.explain: nice() changes a process's scheduling priority; fork() creates a new process, exit() terminates the calling process, and getpid() just returns the process's own ID.

questions.q: In ext3/ext4 journaling, which mode journals only metadata and writes it either before or after the actual data is written to disk, with no strict ordering guarantee?
questions.correct: Writeback mode
distractors: Full data journaling mode (a duplicate of Journal mode)
questions.explain: Writeback mode journals metadata without guaranteeing it happens strictly after data writes, unlike Ordered mode (the default), which enforces data-before-metadata ordering; Journal mode logs both data and metadata.

questions.q: When an interrupt occurs but interrupts are currently masked on the processor, what happens?
questions.correct: Nothing happens until interrupts become unmasked; the interrupt remains pending
distractors: The interrupt is silently discarded and lost forever
The CPU immediately halts until the interrupt is manually cleared
The kernel automatically panics to avoid data loss
questions.explain: A masked interrupt simply waits as pending until unmasking occurs, rather than being lost, halting the CPU outright, or triggering a kernel panic.

questions.q: Which redirection sequence closes file descriptor 2 (stderr) entirely rather than redirecting it somewhere?
questions.explain: `2>&-` closes the referenced file descriptor outright; `2>/dev/null` redirects stderr to the null device (still open, just discarded), `2>&1` merges stderr into stdout, and `&>/dev/null` redirects both stdout and stderr to null.

questions.q: Which redirection correctly sends both stdout and stderr to the same destination in one shorthand, without merging them explicitly with `2>&1`?
questions.correct: &>/dev/null
questions.explain: `&>/dev/null` is bash shorthand for redirecting both streams together; `2>&-` closes stderr, `1>&2` redirects stdout into wherever stderr currently points (not a combined shorthand), and `2>1` is invalid syntax (it would just create a file literally named '1').

questions.q: When redirecting stdout and stderr to two different files in the same command, which syntax appends to both rather than overwriting them?
questions.correct: command 2>> error 1>> output
questions.explain: The `>>` operator specifically appends rather than overwriting; plain `>` (single arrow), as used in the other examples, truncates and overwrites the target file's existing contents.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT one of the four possible port states nmap reports when scanning against a firewall?
questions.correct: Encrypted
questions.explain: nmap's real states in this context are open, closed, filtered, and unfiltered; 'encrypted' isn't a port state nmap reports at all.

questions.q: Which log analysis tool is described as an open-source real-time web log analyzer that can run interactively in a terminal?
questions.correct: goaccess
questions.explain: goaccess is specifically a real-time terminal-based web log analyzer; graylog is a broader log management platform (typically web-UI based), tcpdump captures packets rather than analyzing web logs, and auditd tracks system call auditing.

questions.q: Which command is generally recommended as the safest, most universal way to check available disk space usage by filesystem?
questions.correct: df
questions.explain: df reports filesystem-level free/used space directly; du reports directory/file usage (which can disagree with df in edge cases), fdisk -l shows partition tables, and lsblk shows block device layout, not usage percentages.

questions.q: Which command shows a summary of resource limits (ulimit) currently in effect for the running shell?
questions.correct: ulimit -a
questions.explain: `ulimit -a` prints all current limits for the shell; `-H` alone only toggles hard-limit display for a specific resource, limits.conf isn't a command, and sysctl -a dumps kernel parameters, not shell resource limits.

questions.q: Which command-line tool is purpose-built for querying DNS records and is generally preferred by sysadmins over `nslookup` for detailed lookups?
questions.correct: dig
questions.explain: `dig` gives the most detailed, scriptable DNS query output and is the sysadmin favorite; `host` gives simpler output, and ping/traceroute aren't DNS query tools at all.

questions.q: Which signal, unlike SIGTERM, cannot be caught, blocked, or ignored by a process?
questions.correct: SIGKILL
questions.explain: SIGKILL is specifically designed to be un-catchable and un-ignorable, forcing immediate termination; SIGTERM, SIGHUP, and SIGINT can all be caught or handled by a well-behaved process.

questions.q: Which signal pauses (stops) a process's execution without terminating it, and can later be resumed with SIGCONT?
questions.correct: SIGSTOP
questions.explain: SIGSTOP suspends a process for later resumption via SIGCONT; SIGKILL/SIGTERM terminate the process rather than pausing it, and SIGHUP is used for hangup/reload notifications, not pausing.

questions.q: Which RAID level uses striping with a single distributed parity block, tolerating exactly one drive failure?
questions.correct: RAID5
questions.explain: RAID5 stripes data with one parity block per stripe, surviving a single drive failure; RAID0 has no redundancy, RAID1 mirrors rather than using parity, and RAID6 uses double parity to survive two drive failures.

questions.q: Which RAID level uses double distributed parity, allowing it to survive two simultaneous drive failures?
questions.correct: RAID6
questions.explain: RAID6 extends RAID5's single parity to double parity, tolerating two failed drives; RAID5 tolerates only one, RAID1 relies on mirroring (not parity), and RAID0 offers no redundancy at all.

questions.q: Which port does FTP use for the control connection (as opposed to data transfer)?
questions.explain: FTP control runs on port 21, with port 20 used for the data connection; port 22 is SSH and 23 is Telnet, both unrelated to FTP.

questions.q: Which port does DNS typically use for both queries and zone transfers?
questions.explain: DNS operates on port 53; 67/68 are DHCP server/client ports respectively, and 25 is SMTP.

questions.q: Which chmod octal value corresponds to permissions rwxr-xr-x?
questions.explain: 755 gives the owner full rwx and group/others read+execute (rwxr-xr-x); 644 is rw-r--r--, 777 is full permissions for everyone, and 700 restricts everything to the owner only.

questions.q: Which chmod octal value corresponds to permissions rw-r--r--, a common default for regular files?
questions.explain: 644 grants the owner read+write and group/others read-only (rw-r--r--); 755 adds execute for everyone, 600 restricts read/write to the owner alone, and 666 gives everyone read+write with no execute.

questions.q: Which git command shows which files have been staged with `git add` as well as any further changes since staging?
questions.correct: git status
questions.explain: `git status` reports both staged files and further working-tree changes in one summary view; `git log` shows commit history, `git diff --staged` only shows staged changes without the full status picture, and `git branch` lists branches.

questions.q: Which docker command lists all container images stored locally?
questions.correct: docker images
questions.explain: `docker images` specifically lists locally stored images; `docker ps -a` lists containers (not images), and network ls/volume ls list Docker networks and volumes respectively.

questions.q: Which command-line flag, when used with `ss` or `netstat`, restricts output to listening sockets only?
questions.correct: -l
questions.explain: `-l` filters for listening sockets specifically; `-a` shows all sockets (listening and established), `-n` just avoids resolving names to numbers, and `-p` shows the owning process, none of which filter to listening-only by themselves.

questions.q: Which command displays currently mounted filesystems along with their disk usage, size, and percentage used?
questions.correct: df -h
questions.explain: `df -h` gives a human-readable usage summary per mounted filesystem; plain `mount` lists mount points without usage stats, `du -h` reports directory/file sizes (not filesystem-level usage), and `fdisk -l` shows partition tables.

questions.q: Which command displays a process tree, showing parent-child relationships between running processes?
questions.correct: pstree
questions.explain: `pstree` specifically visualizes the process hierarchy as a tree; `ps aux` lists processes in a flat table, `top` shows a live-updating flat list, and `w` shows logged-in users, not process hierarchy.

questions.q: Which command changes a file's owner and group in a single invocation?
questions.correct: chown user:group file
questions.explain: `chown user:group` sets both owner and group at once; `chmod` sets permission bits (not ownership), `chgrp` only changes the group, and `chattr` changes file attributes like immutability, not ownership.

questions.q: Which command specifically shows the ARP cache, mapping local IP addresses to MAC addresses?
questions.correct: arp -a
questions.explain: `arp -a` displays the ARP table (IP-to-MAC mappings); `route -n` shows the routing table, `netstat -i` shows interface statistics, and `ip link show` lists interfaces without ARP mapping info.

questions.q: Which command lists open files held by a specific running process, identified by PID?
questions.correct: lsof -p <pid>
questions.explain: `lsof -p` lists a given process's open file descriptors; `ps -p` just shows process status info, `fuser` identifies processes using a *file* (not the reverse), and `top -p` just monitors resource usage for a PID.

questions.q: Which command displays the amount of free and used physical and swap memory on a Linux system, in human-readable form?
questions.correct: free -h
questions.explain: `free -h` reports physical/swap memory usage in human-readable units directly; `top -m` isn't a standard top flag for this, `vmstat -h` just shows vmstat's help text rather than memory stats, and `df -h` reports disk (not memory) usage.

questions.q: Which command shows detailed information about block devices and their mount points in a tree-like view?
questions.correct: lsblk
questions.explain: `lsblk` specifically presents a tree view of block devices and where they're mounted; `blkid` reports device UUIDs/filesystem types (no tree view), `fdisk -l` lists partition tables, and `du -sh` summarizes directory sizes, unrelated to block devices.

questions.q: Which command shows real-time network connections along with the process ID and name using them, requiring root privileges for full detail?
questions.correct: lsof -i
questions.explain: `lsof -i` lists network connections tied to processes; ping's `-i` sets the interval between pings, curl's `-i` includes response headers in output, and dig doesn't have an `-i` flag for this purpose - none of them show process-to-connection mappings.

questions.q: Which command tests whether a remote host is reachable at the network layer, without testing any specific application port?
questions.correct: ping
questions.explain: `ping` uses ICMP to test basic network-layer reachability, independent of any application port; telnet, curl, and `nc -vz` all specifically test connectivity to a particular application-layer port/service.

questions.q: Which file typically contains the definitions of local user groups and their members on a Linux system?
questions.correct: /etc/group
questions.explain: /etc/group holds group definitions and membership; /etc/passwd holds user account info (not group membership lists), /etc/shadow holds password hashes, and /etc/gshadow holds group password/admin info as a companion file, not the primary group list.

questions.q: Which protocol automatically assigns IP addresses and network configuration to devices on a LAN?
questions.correct: DHCP
questions.explain: DHCP dynamically assigns IPs and network config; DNS resolves names to addresses, NAT translates addresses (doesn't assign them), and ARP maps IP to MAC addresses on the local segment.

questions.q: Which protocol is responsible for resolving a known IP address to a MAC address on a local network segment?
questions.correct: ARP (Address Resolution Protocol)
distractors: RARP performing the same direction of lookup
questions.explain: ARP maps IP addresses to MAC addresses on the local segment; DHCP assigns IP configuration, ICMP handles diagnostic/error messaging (like ping), and RARP actually performs the reverse lookup (MAC to IP), not the same direction as ARP.

questions.q: Which command displays a live, continuously updating list of open files and network connections, useful for troubleshooting resource leaks?
questions.correct: lsof (optionally combined with watch)
questions.explain: lsof (potentially re-run via watch) is used to inspect open files/connections live; /proc/meminfo is a static memory snapshot, `free -s 1` repeats memory stats (not open files), and `uptime -p` just shows how long the system has been running.

questions.q: Which command changes a file's group ownership without altering the owner?
questions.correct: chgrp
questions.explain: `chgrp` specifically changes only the group; `chown` can change owner (and optionally group together), `chmod` changes permission bits, and `usermod` modifies user account properties, not file ownership.

questions.q: Which command displays the currently running kernel version on a Linux system?
questions.correct: uname -r
questions.explain: `uname -r` specifically prints the kernel release version; `uname -a` gives broader system info (not just hostname, contrary to the distractor), while /etc/os-release and lsb_release describe the distribution, not the kernel version specifically.

questions.q: Which port is the standard default for unencrypted HTTP web traffic?
questions.explain: Port 80 is the classic default for HTTP; 443 is HTTPS, while 8080 and 8443 are common alternate/proxy ports but not the standard defaults.

questions.q: Which port is the standard default for encrypted HTTPS web traffic?
questions.explain: Port 443 is the standard default for HTTPS; 80 is plain HTTP, 8080 is a common alternate HTTP port, and 21 is FTP control.

questions.q: Which command lets you monitor disk I/O activity per process in real time, helping confirm whether I/O wait is causing performance problems?
questions.correct: iotop
questions.explain: `iotop` shows per-process disk I/O in real time; `iostat` (without per-process detail) gives system-wide I/O stats, `vmstat -m` reports slab memory info, and `free -t` just adds a totals line to memory usage, none of which show per-process disk I/O.

questions.q: Which command displays a detailed, real-time breakdown of CPU usage per core, useful for confirming whether load is CPU-bound or I/O-bound?
questions.correct: mpstat -P ALL
questions.explain: `mpstat -P ALL` breaks down CPU usage per core including I/O wait percentage; `uptime -p` only shows system uptime duration, `free -m` shows memory (not CPU) stats, and `df -i` shows inode usage, unrelated to CPU.

questions.q: Which command safely and permanently deletes a file such that its content cannot be recovered by typical file-carving tools, unlike a normal `rm`?
questions.correct: shred
questions.explain: `shred` overwrites file content before removal, resisting recovery; plain `rm -f` (and `unlink`) just removes the directory entry while data may remain recoverable on disk, and `truncate` merely resizes a file rather than securely erasing it.
